opening.headline: This document explains how to distinguish and securely pass the API key used during build, specifying the path preserved in the image.
body: When building AI services, you may need API keys to access private package repositories or model repositories. Passing the key as a build argument or environment variable for convenience can result in the key value remaining directly inside the final image.

In this lesson, we examine what build secrets are, which transfer methods are risky, how to use secret mounts and SSH mounts, and finally, we walk through an example of fixing a secret passed via ARG that appears in the image history.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can describe the distribution method of Build Secrets
Secret can distinguish the path remaining in the image.
Can judge the risk of secret exposure

screens.title: The build secret has been retained in the image layer.
screens.lead: This is a typical scenario that occurs when build secrets are exposed. Select each item to verify what the issue is.

visual.alt: A diagram showing the keys used during build propagating all the way through the image layer list and registry.

items.prompt: The API key used during build can be seen directly when the image is opened.
items.answer: Build parameters and environment variables remain in the final image. Upon receiving the image, someone can open the image configuration or history to read the keys. The fact that values do not disappear after the build completes is the starting point.

items.prompt: At the moment an image is registered in the registry, the key is also dispersed.
items.answer: If a value is already present in the image, at the moment it is written to the registry, the key is delivered to all parties who can receive that image. Even if it is a private registry, the broader access scope means a wider exposure range.

items.prompt: The fact that layers are retained in the history even when deleted is what causes the issue.
items.answer: Even if you delete the file in a later step, the layers created in an earlier step are already embedded within the image. Therefore, you cannot prevent exposure by simply deleting files later on.

screens.outro: The question for this class is this: What is the path by which secret information remains in an image, and how is it blocked?

screens.title: Preview: Methods for passing keys from a build
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts are displayed. Please think about the answer mentally before entering or submitting it.

items.prompt: How do I pass the API key when building?
items.answer: The easiest approach is to pass credentials using `ARG` or `ENV`, and many teams actually start this way. While convenient, it is described as inappropriate for secret transmission because the documentation remains build parameters and environment variables in the final image.

items.prompt: Where will that value reside after the build is complete?
items.answer: Image settings and history may be retained. When an image is registered in the registry, its record is also uploaded. Knowing where values are stored is the first step in assessing risk.

items.prompt: Why does the team use the same approach?
items.answer: This is because it is generally the simplest and most commonly used method going back for a long time. A secure method can also be implemented with just two lines of command. We will now check the secure transfer method on the next screen.

screens.outro: Let's first define and clarify why the delivery method is risky.

screens.title: Definition of Build Secrets and Delivery Methods to Avoid
screens.lead: Select the button to change state and alternately compare risky and secure transfer methods.

visual.alt: The ARG delivery method compares the image persistence of values versus the secret mount, which disappears after the command ends.

states.label: Approaches to avoid: ARG and ENV
states.body:
Build secrets refer to sensitive information such as passwords or API tokens used during the build process. Build arguments (`ARG`) and environment variables (`ENV`) are inappropriate for passing secrets to a build because they remain in the final image.

The persisted information is within the image configuration and its history. When an image is pushed to a registry, this information is also uploaded, allowing anyone who can access the image to read the values. Even if a file is removed in a later stage, the value remains in earlier layers.

states.label: Secure method: Secret mount
states.body:
The document safely guides you through secret mounts and SSH mounts. A secret mount temporarily exposes secrets from the build client inside the build container only during the execution of the build command.

Once the command completes, the mount is removed, so no values remain in the image layer. This is a general approach suitable for tasks requiring keys, such as accessing a private artifact server or API. Use an SSH mount instead when SSH sockets or keys are required.

screens.outro: Secret mount is performed in two steps. Let's verify it by reading the actual command.

screens.title: Secret Mount: Use in Two Steps
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to sequentially read the command to pass and receive the secret, and the Dockerfile line.

visual.alt: Diagram showing the connection between the secret ID of the build command and the mount ID of the Dockerfile.

steps.title: Step 1: Passing secrets in the build command
steps.body: The `docker build --secret id=aws,src=$HOME/.aws/credentials .` command designates the original of the secret with ID `aws` as a file in the build client. At this stage, the value is not embedded into the image; it only informs the builder that it can be read. If Bake is used, the same content is written to the `secret` item in the form of `id=aws,src=`.

steps.title: Step 2: Writing secrets in the Dockerfile
steps.body: `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=aws` hides the secret with the same id only in the `RUN` command. By default, the secret is mounted as a file in the `/run/secrets/<id>` path. This option must be appended to every command that uses the secret.

steps.title: Tool to read the file
steps.body: The following line's `AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE=/run/secrets/aws` causes the AWS tool to read the temporary file below `/run/secrets/` as credentials. If you want to change the location the tool reads from, you can specify the file path using the `target` option, or mount it as an environment variable using the `env` option.

steps.title: If the ID is different, the connection does not establish.
steps.body: The ID of the command must match the ID of the Dockerfile. If the command has ID `id=npm` but the Dockerfile has ID `id=aws`, then the secret lookup at `RUN` fails, resulting in authentication failure. If authentication fails, first verify that the two IDs match.

steps.title: When the original is an environment variable
steps.body: The original of Secret may be a file or an environment variable. If it is an environment variable, it is written as `docker build --secret id=kube,env=KUBECONFIG .`, and within the build container, it appears as the `/run/secrets/kube` file. If the `env` parameter is omitted and written as `--secret id=API_TOKEN`, it will be linked to a file with the same name.

steps.title: Source Type and Reason Images Do Not Remain
steps.body: The source type is automatically detected by CLI and Bake, and may also be explicitly specified using `type=file` or `type=env`. Secrets are mounted only during command execution and are removed once the command completes, so no values remain in the image layers.

screens.outro: For handling a private Git repository, there is SSH mounting and a dedicated authentication secret.

screens.title: SSH Mount and Git Authentication
screens.lead: Select each tab to explore three ways of handling a private Git repository in your build process.

tabs.label: SSH mount
tabs.body:
SSH mounting is a specialized mount that allows SSH sockets or keys to be used within the build environment. It is most commonly used when you need to retrieve a private Git repository during the build process.

For example, a Dockerfile can fetch a repository using `ADD git@github.com:me/myprivaterepo.git /src/`, and pass an SSH socket to the build command using `docker buildx build --ssh default .`. This approach connects only to the socket without copying the key into the image.

tabs.label: Private context
tabs.body:
Using the private Git repository itself as the build context requires authentication information. If `docker build https://github.com/example/todo-app.git` is executed without authentication, the builder fails with a `could not read Username` error because it lacks the permission to read the repository.

This authentication information is used during the step of retrieving the context, not within the build command. Therefore, such secrets are referred to as pre-authentication secrets.

tabs.label: GIT_AUTH_TOKEN
tabs.body:
`GIT_AUTH_TOKEN` creates a basic authentication header using the fixed user `x-access-token`. Providers that adopt this approach operate similarly to GitHub.

For example, a token can be stored in an environment variable and passed as a secret, such as with `GIT_AUTH_TOKEN=$(gh auth token) docker build --secret id=GIT_AUTH_TOKEN https://github.com/example/todo-app.git`. The same secret can also be used when retrieving from a private repository using `ADD`.

tabs.label: GIT_AUTH_HEADER
tabs.body:
`GIT_AUTH_HEADER` uses the provided value directly in the `Authorization` header. This approach works with any Git provider.

GitLab's `CI_JOB_TOKEN` requires basic authentication with a username of `gitlab-ci-token`; however, `GIT_AUTH_TOKEN` always uses `x-access-token` as the username, which is incorrect. In such cases, `GIT_AUTH_HEADER` directly passes a custom header value.

screens.outro: Now let's examine an example of a key transferred to ARG as it appears in the history.

screens.title: Explanation: The key transferred to ARG is illustrated in the history record.
screens.lead: This shows a lecturer reading and correcting a problematic Dockerfile. Select the right arrow to follow along.

visual.alt: A screen displaying the Dockerfile before and after modification side by side.

steps.title: Read setting
steps.body: The Dockerfile receives a key with `ARG API_KEY`, receives a file with `RUN curl -H "Authorization: $API_KEY" -o /tmp/model.bin https://models.example.com/model.bin`, and then deletes the file received at the final step with `RUN` to `rm`. Since both the key and the file are deleted, this configuration appears safe.

steps.title: Step 1: The starting point is the ARG in the first row.
steps.body: The starting point of the issue is `ARG API_KEY`. `ARG` is a delivery method that remains in the final image, so it should not be used in secret contexts. The value does not disappear after the build is complete, and the person who receives the image can verify it.

steps.title: Step 2: The value is displayed in the history.
steps.body: Inspecting the image with `docker history` shows the value available on the command line at `curl`. Although the file was deleted with the last `RUN`, the prior layer and history remain unchanged. Deletion only adds a new layer and does not remove the previous layer.

steps.title: Step 3: Fix with Secret Mount
steps.body: The fixed value starts with `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=api_key` and reads the value from the `/run/secrets/api_key` file. The value is not directly specified in the command line, and the mount is removed when the command ends. The received model file does not need to be deleted and can be saved directly to the required location.

steps.title: Step 4: Change the build command and verify it.
steps.body: The build command is set to `docker build --secret id=api_key,env=API_KEY .`. The key is read from the host's environment variable `API_KEY` and passed as a secret. After building, verify that the history entry has no value at `docker history` to confirm the fix.

steps.title: Step 5: If already compromised, dispose of and replace it.
steps.body: If an image has already been exposed and is present in the registry, simply modifying the Dockerfile is not sufficient. The compromised key must be retired and a new one issued. This is because even if the image is removed, it cannot be ruled out that someone has already obtained it.

screens.outro: Finally, I will summarize the lecture content.

screens.title: Core takeaway: Secret does not bend to images
screens.lead: This course content is summarized in three aspects: delivery method, exposure path, and response.

paragraphs: **Distribution method** consists of two steps. The secret is passed to the build command via `--secret`, and then retrieved by the Dockerfile using `RUN --mount=type=secret`. The value is only visible under `/run/secrets/` during the execution of the command. For private Git repositories, SSH mounts or `GIT_AUTH_TOKEN`, `GIT_AUTH_HEADER` are used.

**Exposure Path** is image configuration, history, and prior layers. `ARG` and `ENV` remain in the final image, and even if they are removed in later stages, the prior layers remain unchanged. When an image is pushed to the registry, this path is propagated together.

Response is prevention and replacement. Transmit immediately using secret mounts, and discard previously exposed values, replacing them with newly issued ones. Habitually checking logs after builds also helps.

glossary.def: Sensitive information such as passwords or API tokens used during the build process.
The secret of the build client is temporarily made visible inside the container only during the execution of a single command.
A dedicated mount that allows SSH sockets or keys to be used during build process. Often used when retrieving from a private Git repository.
Each instruction in a Dockerfile represents a layer in the change history. The content of a previous layer remains even if it is later removed.
This is a pre-authenticated secret used when retrieving a private Git context. It creates basic authentication using the x-access-token as the user.

misconceptions.myth: Once the file is deleted, the secret is also gone.
misconceptions.fact: During the back step, values may still remain in the prior layer and history. It must be passed from the beginning using --mount=type=secret.

misconceptions.myth: Environment variables are safe because they exist only at runtime.
misconceptions.fact: Environment variables and parameters used during build remain in the final image. They are not appropriate for secret transmission.

misconceptions.myth: The value of secret mount is stored in the image.
misconceptions.fact: The mount is displayed only during execution of the command and does not remain in the image.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Secret does not bend to images.
ARG and ENV are already stored in the image, so they are not used.
-- Safely used in two stages: secret transmission and RUN --mount usage.
If exposed, discard the value and replace it.
